summary: Specifies how authors of RFCs in the IAB stream grant the community rights to copy and use their text, and what rights readers get. It asks the IETF Trust to manage them. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Like the matching rules for independent authors, this document says what everyone may do with the text of RFCs written by the Internet Architecture Board.

questions: what are the rights rules for iab stream rfcs
what rights do readers have for iab rfcs
what is the ietf trust role in rfc copyright
subtitle: What authors give, and what readers may do, with the text of RFCs published through the IAB stream.

tldr.problem: As the IETF grew and the IETF Trust took on a role managing intellectual property rights, the rights for RFCs from the IAB stream had to be spelled out.
tldr.mechanism: Authors grant rights as in RFC 5378, readers get the right to make unlimited derivative works with attribution unless the RFC says otherwise, and the IAB asks the IETF Trust to manage this.
tldr.outcome: The copyright rules for IAB stream documents are made identical to those for Independent Submission stream documents.

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: No derivative works, on author request

today: RFC 5745 is an Informational RFC that, per its own text, updates the formal procedures for the rules in RFC 4846. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
The IETF community has become more careful about defining the rights authors grant to the community for copying documents, and the rights the community grants back to readers. Creating the IETF Trust (RFC 4371) increased the need to be explicit.

This document defines the copyright procedures for RFC IAB stream documents and parallels the procedures for IETF-produced documents in RFC 5377 and RFC 5378. The RFC streams are described in RFC 4844. The text is meant to be consistent with the Independent Submission rules in Section 8 of RFC 4846, and to update that section by clarifying the formal procedures the IETF Trust will use.
sections.eli5: People now care more about who may copy what. This note writes down the rules for documents from the Internet Architecture Board.

sections.title: Goals: A Liberal Copyright Policy
sections.content:
The goal of the IAB stream is to publish information from the IAB to the Internet community, and the RFC argues this is best met with a liberal policy. Any reader may use the content in any manner, and the only restriction is that proper credit (attribution) is given. Lawyers call this permitting unlimited derivative works.

A small subset of documents, such as output from other standards bodies, cannot reasonably allow that. Authors may request that such a document permit no derivative works.

The unlimited policy covers all parts of a document, including code, so no separate licensing step is needed to extract and adapt code. Code in a no-derivative-works document may not be extracted and adapted.
sections.eli5: Most of the time you can copy and change the text as long as you say who wrote it. A few documents are marked do-not-change.

sections.title: Rules for Submission and Requests to the IETF Trust
sections.content:
IAB stream authors submit Internet-Drafts to the same IETF repository as other drafts. At submission they grant rights as described in RFC 5378, and may use the form specified for that RFC to ask for publication with no derivative works. Drafts carry boilerplate defined by the IETF Trust that indicates compliance with RFC 5378 and says either that no derivative works are allowed or, as preferred, that unlimited ones are.

The IETF Trust is expected to publish rules granting readers the right to make unlimited derivative works unless the RFC says otherwise. The IAB also asks the Trustees to publicly confirm their willingness to take responsibility for the rights in the IAB stream and to develop the boilerplate. How this is shown in each document is left to the Trust.
sections.eli5: Authors hand in their work with a label saying how it can be reused, and the Trust, which looks after the rights, makes the label and the rules.

sections.title: Patent and Trademark Rules
sections.content:
Contributors use the IETF Internet-Draft process and must follow BCP 9 (RFC 2026 at the time of writing), including disclosing Patent and Trademark issues that are known or reasonably should be known to them. Disclosure of license terms is also requested under BCP 79, which at the time was RFC 3979, updated by RFC 4879.

The IAB stream uses the IETF IPR disclosure mechanism. The IAB would prefer the most liberal terms, without fees or licensing, and non-discriminatory terms are strongly preferred. There are no specific requirements on licensing terms for IAB stream publication.
sections.eli5: If someone owns an idea that the document needs, they must say so. The IAB likes it best when that idea is free to use, but does not force it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The integrity and quality of the IAB stream are the responsibility of the IAB. The RFC states that this document does not change those responsibilities.
sections.eli5: The IAB is still in charge of keeping its documents good and correct, and this note does not change that.
